extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and readers interested in mathematical aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for judging when a mathematical result (theorem, proof, definition, theory, or example) merits the label 'beautiful' according to Gian‑Carlo Rota's phenomenology: beauty is the experience of enlightenment that yields understanding. Includes positive criteria and common misidentifications to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty = enlightenment
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of mathematics is beautiful precisely when it is enlightening — when it reveals or transmits understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rota's central thesis: the felt experience of finally understanding (a sudden conceptual clarity) is the proper mark of mathematical beauty. This is a content-level criterion: beauty is tied to the way a result clarifies previously murky areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is on a par with truth — a property of the result, not merely of the observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat beauty as an attribute intrinsic to the mathematical content rather than purely subjective taste; it is the result's capacity to enlighten that grounds objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is not a metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: When mathematicians call something 'beautiful' they are using the term in a literal, technical sense, not as poetic embellishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing 'beautiful' to a casual compliment; in mathematical practice it signals a specific epistemic achievement (enlightenment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty distinct from elegance (presentation vs content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegance applies to presentation (one can rewrite a proof to be more elegant); beauty applies to content (you cannot make an ugly theorem beautiful simply by rewriting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate judgments about exposition/style from judgments about the underlying mathematical idea. Improving presentation may increase elegance but not necessarily create the content-level enlightenment that constitutes beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem beauty criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem is beautiful when it is short, deep, definitive, and frees a chunk of mathematics from clutter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for theorems that succinctly capture a core fact, have genuine depth, settle or cleanly resolve a body of problems, and simplify or organize surrounding material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof beauty criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is beautiful when it is concise, surprises by an unexpected method, generalizes immediately, and leaves the reader with a feeling of inevitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs for concision, a method that reveals why the result must be true (inevitability), capacity to generalize, and an aesthetically pleasing surprise that contributes to understanding rather than mere trickery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition beauty criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition is beautiful when it captures a previously vague class of objects with a single criterion that turns out to drive subsequent theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A beautiful definition is felicitous and productive: it isolates the right notion and yields theorems and explanations thereafter, showing that the notion was the right lens to see structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory beauty criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory is beautiful when it organizes a wealth of previously unrelated facts (examples: Galois theory, sheaf theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a theoretical framework unifies disparate phenomena, explains them coherently, and thereby provides enlightenment across a domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example beauty criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: An example is beautiful when it is minimal yet decisive — able to separate two notions in a single line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer examples that are parsimonious and illuminating: the least complicated specimen that exhibits the key phenomenon or distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as a heuristic in research
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty serves as a heuristic: mathematicians pursue beautiful conjectures more than ugly ones because beauty correlates with depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use perceived beauty (signs of enlightenment or promising structure) to guide research direction, while recognizing this is a pragmatic cue rather than a formal proof of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychology of recognition (retrospective nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is recognized in retrospect, not in prospect; a result perceived as beautiful is one that, after long acquaintance, one cannot imagine the world without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that the aesthetic judgment often follows understanding and time; immediate surprise is not sufficient. The sense that a structure was 'waiting to be seen' is part of the aesthetic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness (Hardy) is neither necessary nor sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Rota disagrees with Hardy's emphasis on unexpectedness: unexpectedness is neither necessary nor sufficient for mathematical beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate mere surprise with beauty: many surprising results are mere oddities (not enlightening), and many unsurprising results can be deeply beautiful if they provide clarity or unification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common misidentifications to avoid (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five features often wrongly identified with beauty: (1) unexpectedness, (2) brevity, (3) generality, (4) depth, (5) difficulty — each can fail to indicate beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of using brevity, generality, depth, or difficulty as proxies for beauty without checking for actual enlightenment: short proofs can be dull; general results can be unilluminating; deep or difficult results can still be presented or structured in ways that do not enlighten.
